rv.q: A sleek, smart play that lays out issues that were obvious in 1997 – and 1988 and 1959 – is welcome.

Kyoto, by Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson, is so indecently entertaining it almost feels like the result of a bet to choose the dullest, worthiest subject imaginable and make it as fun as humanly possible.
If this is infotainment, it’s infotainment deluxe.

That Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson’s play about the landmark climate change agreement is never remotely dull is a triumph against the odds to match the Protocol itself, even if its success is significantly down to co-director Stephen Daldry.
This dramatisation of it feels “urgent” – and, go on then, I “urge” you to see it.

Kyoto, about the behind-the-scenes battles to create the first global agreement on combating dangerous climate change, is a work of Shakespearean sweep and ambition, an invigorating and challenging piece of political theatre.
Stephen and Justin Martin's production of Kyoto is now a London must see, fitting perfectly into @sohoplace's auditorium.

As urgent and vital as it is, an investigation into international angles on climate change doesn’t sound remotely theatrical, let alone a race-to-the finish thriller. But that is precisely what directors Stephen Daldry and Justin Martin achieve with Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson’s strikingly smart “K...

It’s impossible not to admire the consummate skill with which Murphy and Robertson have compressed almost a decade of fraught debate, giving each meeting a sharp dramatic trajectory that it must have lacked at the time. (In the programme, the late Prescott describes the process as ‘diplomacy by exhaustion’.
Marshalling a company of 20, the directors achieve a degree of vitality that translates into urgency.
The material is extremely dull and yet it’s possible to turn dross into a gripping story if you hire a dramatist.
It’s an exhilarating evening, another slam-dunk for Nimax’s very cool new theatre.
The result is a piece of theatre that is both intellectually stimulating and timely.

cn.t: Critics mostly praise this RSC production for transforming dry climate negotiations into gripping, surprisingly entertaining political thriller. A few find the subject matter inherently dull, but most laud its energy and theatrical craft.
